units.translation: Athena draws from 476 ff. the conclusion: if they remain and do not win, their wrath is terrible, and sending them away at once is not even possible (namely, if Orestes stays here). To this fits ⟦1⟧<⟦2⟧>⟦3⟧ with reference to the first (Scaliger; supported by ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧) and ⟦6⟧ (Dindorf after Butler, who ⟦7⟧. ⟦8⟧) with reference to the second. But since the scholiast explains: ⟦9⟧, a reading diverging more strongly from M has been suspected here, although ⟦10⟧ corresponds to ⟦11⟧, and ⟦12⟧ can be an addition (⟦13⟧ above at 475; ⟦14⟧ ⟦15⟧).
and is in a helpless state
to send them away without wrath is difficult for me
⟦1⟧: so - ~~ ⟦2⟧. 720; cf. ⟦3⟧ in the same verse position ⟦4⟧ (and ⟦5⟧ in another position immediately at 485); also (Dindorf, Poetae scaenici⁵, Preface 35) ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧, 388 ⟦8⟧.
I have power over these matters
V. 481 belongs, like 444, to the verses whose ⟦1⟧ is obscured by elision, to ⟦2⟧.
482 ff. Athena explains her decision: as things stand, the trial must take place despite everything (since sending them away is impossible), but according to 471 not by the goddess herself.

⟦1⟧ is intransitive only here in Aeschylus, and this usage can now be attested only from later authors (⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧), but the simple verb Aeschylus also uses thus: ⟦4⟧. 310 (308) ⟦5⟧ (⟦6⟧), ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧ ⟦9⟧. The scholiast explains ⟦10⟧. After 482 Linwood and Weil assume a lacuna; if, however, with Casaubon one emends ⟦11⟧ to ⟦12⟧ (schol. ⟦13⟧) and ⟦14⟧ to -⟦15⟧, then there is no need for it. The judge also, according to Plato and Aeschylus, has to take the oath; see on 429 ff.;

⟦1⟧ means: I will occupy myself with the selection of judges, in order to create from it a lasting institution (the contrast to the present is ⟦2⟧ 487). Also ⟦3⟧ – is in Aeschylus a quite ordinary position of the article (⟦4⟧), so here 10. 35. 66. 87. 227. 242. 391 ⟦5⟧, etc.; there is nothing to indicate that ⟦6⟧ should be taken as a relative.
⟦1⟧ is at V. 616 the court itself, and can be that here too.
